samples.aliases: austenite-base duplex phase Fe-Mn-Al-C steel (hot rolled + rapidly cooled)

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The forging ingot is homogenized prior to hot rolling.

Hot-rolled to 2–5 mm thickness between 1100 and 850 °C; in some cases reheating among different rolling passes is needed to avoid crack generation. A large rolling reduction provides enough recrystallization driving force, thus inhibiting segregation of FeAl/Fe-Al.

After hot rolling the steel is rapidly cooled to room temperature; the resulting room-temperature microstructure defines the A-BDP classification. The cooling rate after hot rolling strongly influences intergranular κ-carbide formation.

structures.overall_structure: Austenite-base duplex-phase (A-BDP) Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steel produced by hot rolling and rapid cooling to room temperature. This class is defined by the composition window 10.0<X_Mn<25.0, 5.0<X_Al<12.0 and 0.6<X_C<1.0 (wt.%) and its constituent phases are α, B2, DO3, γ, κ-carbide and β-Mn.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: shearing of ordered phases by super-dislocations in ferrite vs. planar slip of dislocations in austenite
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: For the A-BDP Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.8C steel (27% δ-ferrite), nano κ-carbide precipitated in austenite is sheared by plane-slip dislocations during tensile deformation, whereas in ferrite a strong interaction occurs among super-dislocations with narrow mechanical reverse domain boundaries; the strain hardening of A-BDP steels is mainly controlled by shearing of ordered phases by super-dislocations in ferrite and planar slip dislocations in austenite.

interfaces.slip_behavior: In an A-BDP duplex steel (Fe-20Mn-9Al-0.6C), austenite (high SFE) deforms by obvious planar slip on (111) with unidirectional then multidirectional slips and narrowing slip spacing, while ferrite deforms by wavy slip forming dislocation cells.
interfaces.phase_evolution: A-BDP deformation mechanism is strongly affected by the δ-ferrite fraction, the hardness difference between austenite and ferrite, and the ordered phases in ferrite; austenite determines the deformation mechanism when the δ-ferrite fraction is less than 10%.

service_conditions.environment: solution-treated condition (also compared with aging at 550 °C for 16 h)

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: At room temperature the Charpy impact energy of solution-treated A-BDP Fe–Mn–Al–C steels is much higher than typical austenite stainless steel; a ductile-brittle transition occurs below about -100 °C, and after aging at 550 °C for 16 h the room-temperature impact energy decreases significantly (Fe-30Mn-10Al-1C approaches 0 J), attributed to κ-carbide precipitation.

characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy (bright-field TEM) with selected-area electron diffraction (SAED)
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterization of dislocation substructures in austenite and ferrite and identification of nano-scale phases (κ-carbide, B2, DO3) in A-BDP Fe–Mn–Al–C steels.
characterization_methods.key_findings: In an A-BDP Fe-20Mn-9Al-0.6C duplex steel, austenite showed planar slip on (111) (unidirectional at 5%, multidirectional at 10–20%, finer spacing at 40% strain) while ferrite showed wavy slip forming dislocation cells (5% vs 40% strain). In an A-BDP Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.8C steel, fine DO3 particles in ferrite, nano κ-carbide in austenite, and dislocations inside B2 domains after 5% strain were resolved.

unmapped_findings: A-BDP (austenite base duplex phase) steel is defined for Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels after hot rolling and rapidly cooling to room temperature with composition 10.0<X_Mn<25.0, 5.0<X_Al<12.0, 0.6<X_C<1.0 wt.% and constituent phases α, B2, DO3, γ, κ-carbide and β-Mn (Table 1, b0040, b0041).

The aged A-BDP state (aging at 500–800 °C) develops lath-like ferrite along the austenite grain boundaries with B2 phase within the lath-like ferrite, which is distinct from the full-austenite quenched/rapidly-cooled state (b0045).

A-BDP deformation is strongly affected by the δ-ferrite fraction, the hardness difference between austenite and ferrite, and the ordered phases in ferrite; when the δ-ferrite fraction is less than 10% austenite determines the deformation mechanism (b0093, b0094).

The Fe-12Mn-8Al-0.8C A-BDP steel displays a three-stage strain hardening curve separated by critical strains ε₁=0.05 and ε₂=0.30: stage 1 is a sharp drop from single ferrite deformation, stage 2 is approximately linear (austenite starts to deform), and stage 3 is a quick drop due to severe strain localization from the ferrite/austenite hardness difference (b0099).

Frommeyer et al. reported a Fe-26Mn-10Al-C steel with 883 MPa tensile strength and 65% total elongation, where uniform shear deformation of austenite determined the strength-ductility combination (b0098).

In a Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.8C A-BDP steel with 27% δ-ferrite fraction, nano κ-carbide precipitates in austenite under quenching or quenching-ordering annealing and coarsens with increasing ordering-annealing temperature, while coarse B2 and ultrafine DO3 particles precipitate in ferrite (b0101).
For the hot-rolled A-BDP route, the cooling rate after hot rolling strongly influences intergranular κ-carbide formation (b0047).
